analogy.p: Think of a city as a bath. The taps are migration (water pouring in from outside) and the babies born in the city are like a hidden tap inside the bath that keeps adding water. The plughole is deaths and people leaving. When the taps are wide open and the plughole is small, the water level rises quickly, just as a city in a LIC or NEE grows rapidly. As the countryside empties and families have fewer children, the taps slow and the level rises more slowly. The analogy breaks down because people are not identical drops of water: they choose to move because of jobs, services or fear, and their decisions change the city itself.

bullets: **Know:** the two causes of urban growth: rural-urban migration and natural increase.
**Explain:** push factors from rural areas and pull factors to cities using the push-pull model.
**Explain:** why natural increase is high in many cities in LICs and NEEs (young migrants, high birth rate, falling death rate).
**Calculate:** natural increase = birth rate - death rate (per 1000), and convert to a percentage by dividing by 10.
**Understand:** the roles of industrialisation, globalisation and TNCs in creating pull factors.
**Command words:** 'Explain' (reasons with 'because'), 'Describe' (what the data show), 'Calculate' (working and units).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 asks you to understand the **factors affecting the rate of urbanisation**: **migration (push-pull theory)** and **natural increase**. In an exam you must be able to explain why cities in LICs and NEEs grow so quickly, using exact terms, and to link the causes to the opportunities and challenges studied later. You also need to be able to use and calculate natural increase (birth rate minus death rate) and to interpret data on migration and population change.

bullets: **Natural increase:** births minus deaths in the city in a year.
**Net migration:** immigrants (in-migrants) minus emigrants (out-migrants).
**Internal migration:** moves within a country, most commonly rural to urban, which is what drives urbanisation (the percentage urban).
**International migration:** moves between countries (for example into Gulf cities for work), which adds to city growth but does not change urbanisation in the source country in the same way.
**If a question gives data,** check whether the growth in a city is mainly natural or mainly migration; then explain why.
**Over time:** migration usually slows as rural populations shrink and fertility falls, so growth rates decline.
core.h: Urban growth has only two components
core.p: The number of people in a city changes for two reasons: people are **born or die** (natural change) and people **move in or out** (migration). Urban population growth is therefore **natural increase plus net migration**, where net migration means people arriving minus people leaving. In most rapidly growing cities in LICs and NEEs both components are positive and large. Migration often dominates early on, because many people arrive each year, but natural increase becomes more important as migrants settle and start families.

bullets: **Push factors from rural areas:** low and unreliable incomes from subsistence farming; shortage of jobs; few schools, clinics and electricity; drought, flooding or crop failure; desertification and soil exhaustion; land shortages because farms are divided between children.
**Mechanisation** of farming means fewer workers are needed on the land, pushing labourers out.
**Conflict and hazards:** war, persecution, earthquakes or floods can force people to flee, often ending up in a nearby city.

**Pull factors to cities:** more job opportunities (factories, construction, services); higher wages; schools and universities; hospitals and healthcare; piped water, electricity and public transport; entertainment and a perceived better quality of life.
**Social networks (chain migration):** family or friends already in the city provide information, a place to stay and help finding work, so migration builds on itself.
**Perception matters:** migrants may overestimate city opportunities (the 'bright lights' effect); many end up in informal work and squatter settlements.
**Remittances:** money sent home by migrants supports families in rural areas and encourages more people to follow.
core.h: Rural-urban migration and the push-pull model
core.p: **Rural-urban migration** is the movement of people from the countryside into towns and cities. The **push-pull theory** says that migrants are pushed out of one place by negatives (push factors) and pulled to another by positives (pull factors). In many LICs and NEEs, rural life is hard and unreliable, whereas cities offer the hope of regular work and services. People weigh the two and move when the expected benefits of the city seem greater than the costs and risks of leaving.

bullets: **Formula:** natural increase (per 1000) = birth rate - death rate.
**Convert to a percentage:** divide by 10 (22 per 1000 = 2.2%).

**Why birth rates stay high:** limited access to contraception and family planning; children seen as a source of labour and support in old age; high infant mortality (parents have extra children to be safe); cultural and religious beliefs; low levels of female education.
**Why death rates fall:** improved medical care and vaccination, cleaner water, better sanitation, more reliable food supplies, and rising living standards.

**Young population structure:** a large share of the population is under 15 and a large share is of child-bearing age, so the number of births keeps rising even if each woman has fewer children (population momentum).
**Link to the Demographic Transition Model:** many LICs are in stage 2 (high birth rate, falling death rate) and NEEs in stage 3 (birth rate falling), so natural increase is highest in stage 2 and 3.
**Cities vs countryside:** urban birth rates are often lower than rural ones in the long term (better education, contraception, cost of children) but the huge number of young migrants offsets this.
core.h: Natural increase: why it is high in cities in LICs and NEEs
core.p: **Natural increase** is the difference between the **birth rate** and the **death rate**, both measured per 1000 people per year. When birth rates are high and death rates are low, the population grows. In LICs and NEEs, death rates have fallen sharply in recent decades because of improved healthcare, vaccination programmes, clean water, sanitation and better food supply, but birth rates have fallen more slowly. The result is a wide gap and rapid natural increase, which is why populations are growing quickly. Migrants to cities tend to be young adults of child-bearing age, so cities often have higher birth rates than the national average.

bullets: **Selective migration:** more young adults than children or elderly people move, so rural areas lose workers and gain an older population.
**Larger urban labour force:** a young workforce can attract TNCs and fuel industrial growth (a 'demographic dividend' if jobs exist).
**Demand for services:** more babies and children mean a greater need for schools, clinics and housing in the city.
**Gender patterns:** in some regions young men migrate first and send for families later; in others, many young women migrate to work in factories (for example garment factories in Dhaka).
**Rural impacts:** loss of young workers means fewer farm labourers, lower rural productivity and a rising dependency ratio.
**Cycle effect:** migration, births and growth reinforce each other until fertility falls or migration slows.
core.h: Why migrants are mainly young adults and why this matters
core.p: People aged roughly 15 to 35 are most likely to migrate, because they are fit, have fewer responsibilities, are seeking education and work, and are willing to take risks. When they arrive in a city they form relationships and have children, so **migration indirectly drives natural increase**. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle: migration brings young adults, who have babies, which raises the city's population further and keeps the city growing even after migration slows. It also shapes the city's age structure, with a large working-age population and many dependants.

bullets: **Industrialisation:** growth of manufacturing (textiles, electronics, cars) concentrated in cities.

**TNCs** such as clothing and electronics companies locate in cities with cheap labour and good transport links (for example garment factories in Dhaka, Bangladesh, and manufacturing in Shenzhen, China).
**Multiplier effect:** factory jobs create demand for local services (shops, transport, food), generating more jobs and pulling in more migrants.
**Government policy:** special economic zones, tax breaks and investment in ports, roads and airports in particular cities.
**Services and quaternary jobs:** call centres, IT (for example in Bangalore, India) offer higher-paid jobs.
**Urban bias:** most government spending on services, universities and hospitals is in cities, widening the gap with rural areas.
core.h: Industrialisation, globalisation and TNCs as pull factors
core.p: Economic change in NEEs and LICs creates many of the pull factors. **Globalisation** means increasing connections between countries through trade, investment and communication. **Transnational corporations (TNCs)**, which operate in several countries, often build factories, call centres and offices in cities in LICs and NEEs because labour is cheaper, ports and airports are available and governments offer incentives. This creates **formal jobs** and attracts migrants. Governments also invest in infrastructure and education in cities, which makes them even more attractive.

bullets: **Environmental push factors:** drought and crop failure force subsistence farmers to leave; coastal flooding can displace people.
**Conflict and refugees:** people fleeing civil war often move to nearby cities (which are safer or have aid) and can swell their populations quickly.
**Boundary change:** a city's administrative area is enlarged to include peri-urban settlements, increasing the official population.
**Natural disasters** such as earthquakes can destroy rural livelihoods and push people into cities.
**Rural poverty trap:** lack of credit, tools or markets keeps rural incomes low, strengthening the push.
**Evaluation:** which factor is most important differs by country, time and person; a good answer says it depends.
core.h: Other causes: environmental pressures, conflict and reclassification
core.p: Not all rural-urban migration is voluntary. Droughts, floods, desertification and conflict can push people from rural areas. Climate change is increasing some of these pressures, for example droughts in the Sahel or flooding in South Asia. Another cause of apparent urban growth is **reclassification**: when a city boundary expands to include surrounding villages, the official urban population rises even though nobody has moved. Awareness of these extra factors helps with evaluation questions.

bullets: **Early stage:** high migration, high natural increase, cities cannot keep up with demand.
**Middle stage:** industrialisation boosts incomes; migration is strong but birth rates start to fall (DTM stage 3).
**Late stage:** most people already urban; growth driven by natural change and international migration; counterurbanisation may appear in HICs.
**Why slow later:** fewer rural people left, lower fertility, urban living costs and congestion.
**Policy effect:** governments may try to slow rural-urban migration by investing in rural areas (schools, roads, jobs).
**Implication:** cities in LICs and NEEs must plan for decades of growth, which links to sustainability.
core.h: Why growth rates change over time
core.p: Urban growth is rapid in the early stages of development but slows later. At first, many rural people migrate and birth rates are high, so cities grow quickly. As countries develop, **fertility falls** (education, contraception, urban costs of children), **the rural population shrinks** so fewer people are left to move, and cities become more expensive and congested, reducing some pull factors. This explains why HICs urbanised first and have slow growth, whereas LICs and NEEs are in the fast-growth phase. It also explains the S-shaped curve of urbanisation over time.

bullets: **Growth faster than planning:** the number of new arrivals each year outpaces housing and infrastructure.
**Squatter settlements:** built on unused land such as hillsides, floodplains or beside railways; vulnerable to landslides and flooding.
**Informal sector:** many migrants work in street trading, recycling or domestic work, with low incomes and no job security.
**Strain on services:** schools, hospitals, water supplies, waste collection and transport are overwhelmed.
**Environmental effects:** air and water pollution, loss of green space, rising emissions.
**Opportunities:** a growing labour force, new markets, improved services in some areas, remittances, and cultural diversity.
core.h: Consequences that link to the next spec points
core.p: The speed of urban growth creates both opportunities and challenges. Migration and natural increase bring workers, ideas and economic activity, but they also cause **housing shortages**, because the supply of formal housing cannot keep pace with demand. Many migrants build or rent poor-quality homes in **squatter settlements** (informal settlements, shanty towns, slums, favelas), which often lack clean water, sanitation, electricity and secure land tenure. Understanding the causes of growth explains why these problems appear and why they are hard to solve quickly.

bullets: **Natural increase (per 1000)** = birth rate - death rate. Example: 30 - 8 = 22 per 1000.
**As a percentage:** 22 / 10 = 2.2% per year.
**Population after one year of growth** = start x (1 + percentage / 100). Example: 12 million x 1.025 = 12.3 million.
**Two years of growth** = start x 1.025 x 1.025 = 12.6075 million (about 12.61 million).
**Share of growth from migration** = (growth due to migration / total growth) x 100.
**Describing graphs:** identify trend, quote values with units, comment on the gap between lines (for example birth rate minus death rate).
**Check:** does your answer make sense (a natural increase cannot be more than the birth rate)?
core.h: Calculations, graphs and data skills for this point
core.p: Examiners often give you a table of birth and death rates or a graph of migration and natural change. The key skills are calculating natural increase, converting it into a percentage, and calculating population after growth. For compound growth, multiply by (1 + rate) for each year. State units (per 1000, %, millions) and show each step so you can earn method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

bullets: **Structure for 4 marks:** Cause 1 (migration) with push and pull, Cause 2 (natural increase) with reasons, each linked using 'because'.
**Structure for 6 marks:** introduce the two causes, explain several push and pull factors with development, explain natural increase, link them (young migrants) and give a conclusion.
**Use evidence:** quote numbers from a source if given, or a named city fact if free-response.
**Avoid vague phrases** such as 'because there are more jobs' without saying where, why and how that attracts migrants.
**Balance:** if asked which is more important, compare migration and natural increase and say how the answer changes over time.
**Link forward:** mention the resulting opportunities and challenges briefly to show wider understanding.
core.h: Putting it together in exam answers
core.p: A top-band answer on the causes of urban growth names both causes, develops each with specific factors, links them through the idea of young migrants having children, and finishes with a judgement. Always use geographical terms accurately and, where possible, use a named example from your LIC/NEE city (for example Lagos or Rio de Janeiro) to show that the factors are real. For 'explain' questions use connectives such as 'because', 'which means' and 'as a result'.

exam: **Command words:** 'Explain' needs reasons developed with 'because'; 'Describe' needs what the data show; 'Calculate' needs working and units.
**1 mark:** define a term (for example 'natural increase') or give one push or pull factor.
**2 marks:** a factor with development (for example 'Mechanisation of farms, so fewer jobs in the countryside').
**3 marks:** two linked points or a calculation plus a short explanation.
**4 marks:** explain two causes (migration and natural increase) with developed push/pull or birth/death rate reasons.
**6 marks:** balanced, structured explanation with named example from an LIC/NEE city, linked ideas and a conclusion.
**Model phrases:** 'which means that', 'as a result', 'this is because', 'in contrast', 'this leads to'.
**Calculations:** write the formula, substitute numbers, give the answer with units; for percentages divide per 1000 by 10.
**Graph/data tips:** quote values with units, compare gaps between birth and death rates, and say whether natural increase is rising or falling.
**Evaluate questions:** weigh migration against natural increase and say which matters more and when.

mistakes.r: There are two causes: rural-urban migration AND natural increase (births minus deaths), and migrants' children add to growth.
mistakes.w: Urban growth is only caused by people moving to cities.

mistakes.r: Develop it: name the type of jobs (factory work, construction), say wages are higher and more reliable than subsistence farming, and link to TNCs.
mistakes.w: People move to cities because there are more jobs.

mistakes.r: Natural increase = birth rate MINUS death rate.
mistakes.w: Natural increase = birth rate + death rate.

mistakes.r: Per 1000 must be divided by 10 to give a percentage: 22 per 1000 = 2.2%.
Push factors are negatives of the origin (drought, poverty); pull factors are positives of the destination (jobs, schools).
mistakes.w: Mixing push and pull factors (saying 'drought pulls people').

mistakes.r: Death rates have fallen because of healthcare and sanitation; birth rates remain high so population is rising.
mistakes.w: Death rates are rising in LICs so population is falling.

mistakes.r: Use 'because...' chains: for example 'Machines replace workers, which means fewer farm jobs, so people migrate to find work'.
Show the working, include per 1000 or %, and set the working out step by step.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or percentage conversion in calculations.

summary: The specification asks you to explain the factors affecting the rate of urbanisation: migration (push-pull theory) and natural increase, plus the roles of industrialisation and globalisation. You must also be able to calculate natural increase, because it explains why cities in LICs and NEEs grow so quickly and why that growth creates challenges.

terms.d: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities.
A negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave it, for example drought or lack of jobs.
A positive aspect of a place that attracts people to it, for example jobs, schools and hospitals.
The growth in population that occurs when the birth rate is higher than the death rate.
The number of live births per 1000 people in a population per year.
The number of deaths per 1000 people in a population per year.
The difference between the number of people moving into an area and the number moving out.
The increasing connections between countries through trade, investment, communication and movement of people.
A company that operates in more than one country, often with factories or offices in LICs and NEEs.
The growth of manufacturing industry in a country or region.
When new jobs and income in one industry create demand for goods and services, leading to further jobs and growth.
Farming where the crops and animals produced are used mainly to feed the farmer's own family.
Money sent home by migrants to their families.
An area of informal, often self-built housing on land the occupants do not legally own, often lacking basic services.
Jobs that are not regulated or taxed by the government and have no formal contract.
The number of babies per 1000 live births who die before their first birthday.
When migrants follow friends or family to a place where relatives have already settled.

worked.q: A city in an NEE has a birth rate of 30 per 1000 and a death rate of 8 per 1000. Calculate the natural increase as a percentage. (2 marks)
steps: Natural increase per 1000 = birth rate - death rate = 30 - 8 = 22 per 1000.
Convert to a percentage by dividing by 10: 22 / 10 = 2.2%.

worked.ans: About 12.61 million people after two years.
worked.q: A city of 12 million people is growing at 2.5% a year. Calculate its population after two years. Give your answer in millions to 2 decimal places. (3 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: Cities in LICs and NEEs are growing because of rural-urban migration and natural increase. Many rural areas have push factors such as low incomes from subsistence farming, drought and mechanisation, which means fewer farm jobs. Cities have pull factors such as jobs in factories and offices created by TNCs, higher wages and better access to schools and hospitals, so people migrate. Because migrants are mostly young adults, they have children in the city, and natural increase is high as death rates have fallen due to better healthcare while birth rates remain high. This means growth continues even if migration slows. Overall, migration is the main driver in the early stages, but natural increase becomes more important in the long term.
worked.q: Explain why cities in LICs and NEEs are growing rapidly. (6 marks)
steps: Migration: rural push factors (low farm incomes, mechanisation, drought, few services) combine with urban pull factors (factory and service jobs, higher wages, schools, hospitals).
TNCs and globalisation create formal jobs, and the multiplier effect creates further jobs and more migrants.
Natural increase: death rates have fallen due to healthcare and sanitation, but birth rates remain high because of limited family planning and the need for children as workers and carers.
Link: migrants are mostly young adults who have children in the city, so natural increase adds to growth.
Conclusion: migration is probably dominant at first, but natural increase becomes increasingly important as migrants settle.
